questions.q: Define verbal irony and give one example from "My Watch" where the narrator says the opposite of what he means.
questions.a: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says something but means the opposite, often for humorous or critical effect. In "My Watch", the narrator says, "I took it to the watchmaker to be regulated" after it has already been ruined by previous repairs, implying he expects a simple fix when the situation is hopeless. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing verbal irony with sarcasm or missing the contrast) shows the student cannot distinguish the device from tone or cannot locate textual evidence.

questions.q: Explain the difference between situational irony and dramatic irony. Which one dominates in "My Watch"? Justify with two textual details.
questions.a: Situational irony arises when outcomes contradict expectations; dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows more than the characters. "My Watch" is driven by situational irony: the narrator expects each repair to improve the watch, but each makes it worse (e.g., the watch runs too fast, then too slow, then stops entirely). A wrong answer that picks dramatic irony reveals the student misunderstands the narrative perspective (first-person narration limits dramatic irony) or cannot map the concept to the plot.

questions.q: Apply the concept of symbolism: The watch in the essay is a symbol. What abstract idea does it represent? Support your answer with two specific stages of the watch's deterioration.
questions.a: The watch symbolizes the human desire for order and control over time. Initially it keeps perfect time (order), but after each repair it becomes more erratic (loss of control), finally stopping altogether (futility). A weak answer that only says "it represents time" without linking to the stages of deterioration shows the student cannot connect symbol to narrative arc.

questions.q: Analyze how Twain uses the watchmaker characters (the first watchmaker, the second, the third) to deepen the irony. What pattern emerges?
questions.a: Each watchmaker represents false expertise: they confidently diagnose and "fix" the watch, but their interventions compound the problem. The pattern—expert intervention → increased chaos—creates a cumulative situational irony that satirizes blind faith in authority. A student who merely lists the watchmakers without analyzing the pattern fails to see the structural irony.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the ending: the narrator throws the watch away. Does this resolve the irony or amplify it? Argue your position with evidence.
questions.a: The ending amplifies the irony: the narrator abandons the very object he spent the essay trying to master, admitting defeat to the chaos he sought to control. The watch, symbol of order, is discarded, underscoring the theme that time cannot be tamed. A response that calls it a "happy resolution" misses the ironic tone and thematic depth.

questions.q: Create a new symbolic object for a modern version of this essay (e.g., a smartphone) and write a 3-sentence paragraph showing situational irony in its "repair".
questions.a: Example: "My smartphone was meant to organize my life. After each update it slowed down, froze, and finally deleted my calendar. I threw it in the river and bought a paper planner." A poor answer would lack the irony (e.g., just describing a broken phone) or fail to establish the symbol (the phone as control).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Irony is a literary device where the intended meaning of words is opposite to their literal meaning, or where there is a contrast between ______ and reality.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are telling a friend about a time you tried to fix ______ simple but made it worse—like tightening a loose screw until the whole thing falls apart.
What is Irony? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Irony is a literary device where the intended meaning of words is opposite to their literal meaning, or where there is a contrast between expectation and reality.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Irony?
questions.a: Students often confuse irony with mere coincidence or bad luck.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify at least two instances of irony (verbal, situational, dramatic) and two symbols in "My Watch", explain their function in the essay, and write a structured analytical paragraph using the PEEL method linking device to theme.
